units.title: Waves with Calculus
units.blurb: The wave function, the wave equation, wave energy, phase and interference, and sound.

units.title: Wave Optics
units.blurb: Huygens' principle, polarization by reflection, intensity patterns, resolution and interferometers.

units.title: Images and Optical Instruments
units.blurb: Lens design, two-lens systems, the eye, microscopes and telescopes.

units.title: Special Relativity
units.blurb: Light's constant speed, time dilation, length contraction, the Lorentz transformation, and relativistic energy and momentum.

units.title: The Quantum World
units.blurb: Blackbodies, Compton scattering, the hydrogen atom, uncertainty, wave functions and the Schrödinger equation.

units.title: Nuclei and Particles
units.blurb: Nuclear size and binding, the decay law, reaction energies, dating, and the particles and forces of the Standard Model.

topics.title: The Wave Function y(x, t)
topics.short: A sinusoidal wave is y = A sin(kx − ωt), with k = 2π/λ, ω = 2πf and speed v = ω/k.
topics.trouble: Students think y = A sin(kx + ωt) travels toward +x.

topics.title: The Wave Equation
topics.short: Any shape moving at speed v satisfies ∂²y/∂x² = (1/v²)·∂²y/∂t².
topics.trouble: Students think only sine waves solve the wave equation.

topics.title: Energy and Power of a Wave
topics.short: A wave on a string carries power P = ½μω²A²v, so doubling the amplitude carries four times the power.
topics.trouble: Students think a wave's power grows in proportion to its amplitude.

topics.title: Phase Difference and Interference
topics.short: Two equal waves with phase difference φ add to amplitude 2A cos(φ/2), and a path difference Δr gives φ = 2πΔr/λ.
topics.trouble: Students treat a half-wavelength path difference as constructive, mixing up path and phase.

topics.title: Standing Waves as Two Traveling Waves
topics.short: Two opposite traveling waves add to y = 2A sin kx cos ωt, with nodes that never move.
topics.trouble: Students think the nodes of a standing wave drift along the string.

topics.title: Sound as a Pressure Wave
topics.short: Sound is a pressure wave moving at v = √(B/ρ); pressure nodes sit where the displacement swings most.
topics.trouble: Students think the pressure and the displacement of a sound wave peak at the same places.

topics.title: Beats
topics.short: Two tones of nearly equal frequency throb at the beat frequency |f₁ − f₂|.
topics.trouble: Students add or average the two frequencies to find the beat frequency.

topics.title: Shock Waves
topics.short: A source faster than sound drags a cone of wavefronts with sin θ = v_sound/v_source.
topics.trouble: Students think a sonic boom happens only at the moment a plane passes the speed of sound.

topics.title: Huygens' Principle
topics.short: Every point on a wavefront acts as a source of wavelets, which explains refraction and diffraction.
topics.trouble: Students think diffraction and refraction need two separate explanations.

topics.title: Polarization by Reflection
topics.short: Light reflected at Brewster's angle, tan θ_B = n₂/n₁, is completely polarized.
topics.trouble: Students measure Brewster's angle from the surface instead of the normal.

topics.title: Intensity in Interference Patterns
topics.short: Two slits give I = I₀cos²(πd sin θ/λ), and more slits make sharper bright lines.
topics.trouble: Students think adding slits makes the bright lines wider, when it makes them narrower and brighter.

topics.title: Single-Slit Envelopes and Missing Orders
topics.short: A single slit's pattern sets the envelope of a double-slit pattern, and some bright orders vanish.
topics.trouble: Students treat a double slit as if each slit were a point, ignoring the width of the slits.

topics.title: Resolution and the Rayleigh Criterion
topics.short: Two points can just be told apart when their angular separation is θ = 1.22λ/D.
topics.trouble: Students think enough magnification can reveal any detail.

topics.title: The Michelson Interferometer
topics.short: Moving one mirror a distance λ/2 shifts the pattern by one whole fringe.
topics.trouble: Students count a mirror shift of λ as one fringe, forgetting the light travels the extra distance twice.

topics.title: Antireflection Coatings and Air Wedges
topics.short: A quarter-wave coating cancels a reflection, and counting fringes in an air wedge measures tiny thicknesses.
topics.trouble: Students use the wavelength in air instead of in the coating to find its thickness.

topics.title: X-Ray Diffraction and Bragg's Law
topics.short: Crystal planes a distance d apart reflect X-rays strongly when 2d sin θ = mλ.
topics.trouble: Students measure θ from the normal, as in Snell's law, instead of from the crystal planes.

topics.title: The Lensmaker's Equation
topics.short: A lens's focal length comes from its shape and material: 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂).
topics.trouble: Students give the back surface's radius the wrong sign.

topics.title: Two-Lens Systems
topics.short: The image made by the first lens is the object for the second, and the magnifications multiply.
topics.trouble: Students measure the second object distance from the first lens instead of the second.

topics.title: The Eye and Corrective Lenses
topics.short: A lens's power is P = 1/f in diopters; nearsighted eyes need diverging lenses and farsighted eyes converging ones.
topics.trouble: Students think nearsighted people need converging lenses because they can't see far away.

topics.title: Magnifiers and Microscopes
topics.short: A magnifier gives M = 25 cm/f, and a microscope multiplies the objective's magnification by the eyepiece's.
topics.trouble: Students add the two magnifications instead of multiplying them.

topics.title: Telescope Optics
topics.short: A refracting telescope magnifies by M = −f_objective/f_eyepiece, and its aperture sets how faint and how fine it can see.
topics.trouble: Students think a telescope's magnification is what lets it see faint objects.

topics.title: The Postulates of Relativity
topics.short: The laws of physics and the speed of light are the same in every inertial frame.
topics.trouble: Students think light from a moving source travels faster than c.

topics.title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
topics.short: Two events at the same time in one frame can happen at different times in another.
topics.trouble: Students think "at the same time" means the same thing to every observer.

topics.title: Time Dilation
topics.short: A moving clock runs slow: Δt = γΔτ, with γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²).
topics.trouble: Students apply γ backward, making the proper time the longer one.

topics.title: Length Contraction
topics.short: A moving object is shorter along its motion: L = L₀/γ.
topics.trouble: Students shrink lengths at right angles to the motion too.

topics.title: The Lorentz Transformation
topics.short: x′ = γ(x − vt) and t′ = γ(t − vx/c²) convert events between frames.
topics.trouble: Students drop the vx/c² term, which carries the relativity of simultaneity.

topics.title: Spacetime Diagrams and the Interval
topics.short: The interval s² = (cΔt)² − Δx² is the same for every observer.
topics.trouble: Students think distances and times both change but nothing stays the same between frames.

topics.title: Relativistic Velocity Addition
topics.short: Velocities combine as u′ = (u − v)/(1 − uv/c²), so no speed passes c.
topics.trouble: Students add speeds the everyday way and get more than c.

topics.title: The Relativistic Doppler Effect
topics.short: Light from an approaching source arrives at f = f₀√((1 + β)/(1 − β)), with β = v/c.
topics.trouble: Students use the sound Doppler formula for light, which treats source and observer differently.

topics.title: Relativistic Momentum and Energy
topics.short: p = γmu and E = γmc², linked by E² = (pc)² + (mc²)².
topics.trouble: Students write the kinetic energy as ½mv² at speeds near c, or as γmc² without subtracting mc².

topics.title: Planck and Blackbody Radiation
topics.short: Planck's quantized energies explain the blackbody spectrum, and Wien's and Stefan's laws follow from it.
topics.trouble: Students think the ultraviolet catastrophe was something measured, rather than a failed prediction of classical physics.

topics.title: The Compton Formula
topics.short: Conserving energy and momentum gives Δλ = (h/mc)(1 − cos θ).
topics.trouble: Students use the photon's wavelength in place of the electron's Compton wavelength h/mc.

topics.title: The Bohr Model of Hydrogen
topics.short: Quantized angular momentum gives E_n = −13.6 eV/n² and r_n = n²a₀.
topics.trouble: Students think the n = 1 level has the highest energy because it comes first.

topics.title: Hydrogen's Spectral Series
topics.short: Lyman, Balmer and Paschen lines follow 1/λ = R(1/n_f² − 1/n_i²).
topics.trouble: Students swap n_f and n_i, getting a negative wavelength or the wrong series.

topics.title: The Uncertainty Principle
topics.short: Δx·Δp ≥ ħ/2: the more sharply a position is fixed, the more spread its momentum must have.
topics.trouble: Students think the uncertainty comes from clumsy measuring tools that better tools could fix.

topics.title: Wave Functions and Probability
topics.short: |ψ|² is a probability density, normalized so the total probability is 1.
topics.trouble: Students think ψ itself, rather than |ψ|², is the probability.

topics.title: The Schrödinger Equation
topics.short: −(ħ²/2m)ψ″ + Uψ = Eψ: check whether a function solves it and read off its energy.
topics.trouble: Students think any smooth function is an allowed wave function, forgetting the boundary conditions.

topics.title: A Particle in a Box
topics.short: Confining a particle to a length L allows only E_n = n²h²/(8mL²).
topics.trouble: Students think the lowest energy of a particle in a box is zero.

topics.title: Finite Wells and Tunneling
topics.short: Wave functions leak into barriers, so a particle can tunnel through one with probability about e^(−2κL).
topics.trouble: Students think a particle can never be found where its energy is less than the potential energy.

topics.title: The Quantum Harmonic Oscillator
topics.short: The energies are evenly spaced, E_n = (n + ½)ħω, starting from a nonzero zero-point energy.
topics.trouble: Students think a quantum oscillator can sit perfectly still at its lowest energy.

topics.title: Quantum Numbers in Hydrogen
topics.short: The labels n, l, m_l and m_s name each state, and shell n holds 2n² states.
topics.trouble: Students think l can equal n.

topics.title: Electron Spin and the Exclusion Principle
topics.short: No two electrons in an atom share all four quantum numbers, which builds the periodic table.
topics.trouble: Students think spin means the electron is a tiny ball literally turning.

topics.title: Conductors, Insulators and Semiconductors
topics.short: Energy bands and the gaps between them decide how a solid conducts, and doping and LEDs follow from them.
topics.trouble: Students think semiconductors conduct worse when warmed, as metals do.

topics.title: Nuclear Size and Binding Energy per Nucleon
topics.short: Nuclei have radius R = r₀A^(1/3), and the binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron.
topics.trouble: Students think bigger nuclei are always more tightly bound.

topics.title: The Exponential Decay Law
topics.short: N = N₀e^(−λt), the activity is A = λN, and the half-life is ln 2/λ.
topics.trouble: Students mix up the decay constant with the half-life, or the activity with the number of nuclei.

topics.title: Energy in Nuclear Reactions
topics.short: Q = (mass before − mass after)c², at 931.5 MeV for each atomic mass unit.
topics.trouble: Students mix nuclear masses with atomic masses and lose track of the electrons.

topics.title: Radioactive Dating
topics.short: The fraction of a parent isotope left gives an age: t = (T½/ln 2)·ln(N₀/N).
topics.trouble: Students try carbon dating on rocks millions of years old, far beyond its range.

topics.title: Leptons, Hadrons and Quarks
topics.short: Leptons are fundamental, baryons hold three quarks and mesons a quark and an antiquark.
topics.trouble: Students think protons and neutrons are fundamental particles.

topics.title: Antiparticles, Pair Production and Annihilation
topics.short: Making an electron–positron pair takes at least 2mc², and annihilation turns the pair back into gamma rays.
topics.trouble: Students think a single photon can turn into a pair in empty space, where momentum can't be conserved.

topics.title: Conservation Laws in Particle Reactions
topics.short: Charge, baryon number and lepton number decide which reactions can happen.
topics.trouble: Students allow any reaction whose charges balance, forgetting baryon and lepton number.

topics.title: The Four Forces and Their Carriers
topics.short: Gravity, electromagnetism and the weak and strong forces; the last three are carried by photons, W and Z bosons and gluons.
topics.trouble: Students think the strong force acts between electrons and nuclei.
